title: Newton's Second Law Along an Axis
short: Add the forces along an axis with signs, then a = ΣF/m.
trouble: Students use only the applied force instead of the net force.

blocks.html: Newton's Second Law: F = ma gave $F = ma$. When several forces act, which $F$? The answer is the net force, the sum of all the forces on your free-body diagram, with signs. When that sum is zero, there is no acceleration.
$\Sigma F_x = ma_x$: choose a positive direction, add every force along that axis with its sign, then divide by the mass.

Each force on an object contributes to its acceleration, and forces along a line simply add, with opposite directions subtracting. The object responds to the total, so only the net force sets the acceleration. A large push opposed by large friction can give a small acceleration.

blocks.name: ph-dynamics

opts.task: Change the push and the friction. The acceleration follows the net force (push minus friction), not the push alone.

blocks.cap: A 2 kg cart pushed with 8 N against 3.9 N of friction accelerates at (8 − 3.9)/2 ≈ 2.0 m/s².

items: Draw the free-body diagram and choose a positive direction (usually the direction of the acceleration).
Write $\Sigma F_x$: every force along the axis, with its sign.
Set it equal to $ma_x$ and solve for the unknown.
If forces act along $y$ too, do the same there, separately.

blocks.title: Two opposite forces
blocks.q: A $5\ \text{kg}$ cart is pulled right with $30\ \text{N}$ and left with $12\ \text{N}$. Find its acceleration (right is $+$).

blocks.title: Vertical forces
blocks.q: A $50\ \text{kg}$ model rocket has $800\ \text{N}$ of thrust. Find its acceleration.

blocks.title: Finding a force
blocks.q: What horizontal pull gives a $10\ \text{kg}$ box an acceleration of $1.5\ \text{m/s}^2$ against $20\ \text{N}$ of friction?
steps: $F = 35\ \text{N}$: $20\ \text{N}$ to cancel friction and $15\ \text{N}$ to accelerate.

blocks.html: Using only the applied force in $F = ma$ and forgetting friction, weight or other forces. Check: list every arrow on the free-body diagram along the axis of motion, and make sure each one is in your sum with its sign.
Try it in the Science Lab: The Second Law: F = ma.
